..
As of 209 AM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Large high pressure will slowly shift eastward
through mid week with flow becoming more southerly. This will
result in a warming trend today through Wednesday although some
shower chances towards the Canadian border Tuesday afternoon may
stunt warmth locally. The warmest day will be Wednesday with
deep layer winds advecting warm air out of the
south/southeasterly directions under mostly clear to partly
cloudy skies. As such, highs will be in the low to mid 60s for
most spots today except for southern Vermont where some upper
60s are possible. Tuesday will be similar to today, except
towards the Canadian border where cloud cover and showers may
keep temperatures down in the lower 60s. Upper 60s to low/mid
70s are anticipated for Wednesday under this pattern. A few
spots could exceed their daily records. Overnight lows will 
also remain warmer than typical only dropping into the 40s to 
around 50 tonight and increasing into the upper 40s to mid 50s 
by Wednesday night. 

A weak wave will be moving along the ridge's northern periphery
Tuesday and Tuesday night bringing shower chances mainly to
northern New York and the northern half of Vermont. Amounts will
be light given that it will be moving into a ridge, but QPF has
trended slightly upward to around 0.1" along the Highway 11 
corridor in northern New York. Generally, a couple hundredths 
up to around a tenth of an inch of rain is expected. 

KEY MESSAGE 2: On Thursday, rain will spread eastward through our 
region. It will be driven by an occluded front, which will be tied 
to a well defined but decaying low pressure system over the western 
Great Lakes region heading northeastward. This pattern leads to 
widespread rain but with only modest wind fields and rainfall rates, 
so no hazardous weather is expected at this time. Forecast soundings 
show a sliver of instability insufficient for any thunder, and while 
there will be anomalous moisture, warm cloud depth is limited. 
Rainfall totals through Friday morning from a multi-model blend look 
favored to range from about 0.25" to 0.5" with localized higher 
amounts, most likely occur in the western Adirondack region and 
perhaps the western slopes of the northern Greens. PoPs are only 
limited by timing differences, so for a given six hour period 
chances of rain are generally 60-80% during this period. I would say 
in contrast, for the event overall there is >99% chance of rain 
areawide with about a 75-90% chance of reaching 0.1" of rain.

Many ensemble solutions continue to show a low pressure area develop 
downstream of the incoming upper level low that digs southeastward 
into western New York by Friday night. As this occurs, the 
orientation of the trough becomes negatively tilted; if this happens 
quickly enough as shown in an unlikely scenario favored by 40% of 
GEFS membership, a retrograding/pivoting area of moderate to heavy 
rain initially to our east will retrograde and pivot northwestward 
on Saturday as low pressure moves northward and passes to our east. 
The current operational GFS solution is near the "reasonable high 
end" at the moment amongst the aforementioned GEFS members, in which 
24 hour rainfall amounts could be as high as two inches in portions 
of eastern Vermont. On top of the rain that falls earlier in the 
week, a beneficial rainfall of up to 3" could occur; 1" to 2" is 
more likely across most of Vermont and Adirondacks, and near 1" in 
the rest of northern New York. A slower scenario of the 
aforementioned upper level low will give us a break in rain for much 
of Friday and Saturday before showers return on Sunday. This 
incoming trough will put an end to our above normal temperatures, 
although cloud cover will prevent nighttime conditions from getting 
too chilly.
